translation: Indeed, when the king’s daughter saw that Apollonius was so well trained in all good accomplishments, her heart fell in love with him. Then, after the end of the banquet, the maiden said to the king: ‘Dear father, a little while ago you allowed me to give Apollonius whatever I wished from your treasure.’ King Arcestrates said to her: ‘Give him whatever you wish.’

She then went out very gladly and said: ‘Master Apollonius, with my father’s permission I give you two hundred pounds of gold, and four hundred pounds by weight of silver, and the greatest portion of precious clothing, and twenty male slaves.’ And she then spoke thus to the slaves: ‘Carry these things with you, which I promised Apollonius my teacher, and put them in the chamber in front of my friends.’

This was then done in this way, according to the princess’s command; and all the men who saw them praised her gifts. Then the banquet ended, and all the men rose and took leave of the king and the princess, wished them well, and went home. Apollonius likewise said: ‘You good king and one who has mercy on the poor, and you princess, lover of learning, may you be well.’
He also looked toward the slaves whom the maiden had given him, and said to them: ‘Take with you these things which the princess gave me, and let us go and seek our lodging, so that we may rest.’
interpretive_notes: The first wæs getogen is education/training, not literal pulling; gefēoll hiere mōd on his lufe is rendered as falling in love.

The gifts are the object of gesāwon, and the men are the relative-clause subject. The source’s original note supplies this antecedent analysis, so it is not independently discovered or suitable for an unaided antecedent test.
The original’s cwēn denotes the princess here; calling her queen would obscure the established daughter relationship.
The source has noun genitive plural ðēowa, without an adjective r, in the quantity expression. Twenty male slaves reflects ðēowa manna and their unfree status.
Grētton at the departure is take leave of; bǣdon hīe gesunde bēon expresses a farewell wish. The subsequent bēon gē gesunde is a plural present subjunctive wish, not an infinitive.
Gān wē is a first-plural present subjunctive exhortation. Sēcean is an infinitive with the motion verb; geręstan is reflexive rest with accusative ūs.
